**The Ladder**

Among the things my father left behind was a list. It was on the back of an envelope from the electric company, written in the blue ballpoint he kept in the kitchen drawer with the rubber bands and the dead batteries he never threw out. Eleven items. Some crossed off, most not.

*Fix gate latch.*
*Return ladder to Dave.*
*Call Ruth re: Thursday.*
*Oil — 5W-30.*
*Bank.*
*Ask about the tree.*

Those were the unfinished ones. The finished ones I could read through the strike-lines: *dentist*, *propane*, *stamps*, *pay Marisol*. Marisol was the woman who cleaned every other week. I knew her. The dentist I could figure out. Stamps and propane explained themselves.

But I did not know a Dave, and I did not know a Ruth, and I did not know which tree, or what about it he had meant to ask, or of whom.

I want to be clear that I didn't set out to finish the list. I'm not that kind of person and I don't think he was either. He would have found the idea embarrassing—the son, bereaved, making a pilgrimage of the hardware store. What happened was smaller than that. I was in the house for the week it took to sort things, and the gate latch actually was broken, and it rattled in the wind at night, and on the second day I found a bag of screws in the garage and fixed it. It took twenty minutes. I didn't think about the list until I came back inside and saw the envelope on the counter, and then I felt something I can only describe as a kind of trespass, as if I'd walked into a room that was still his.

The ladder was in the garage too. Aluminum, extension type, the kind that goes up to a second-story gutter. It had a piece of masking tape on one rail with *D. HOLLIS* written in marker, not my father's handwriting. So there was a Dave. Dave Hollis. I didn't know him, but my father had, well enough to borrow his ladder and not well enough, apparently, to give it back before he ran out of Thursdays.

I looked him up. There was a D. Hollis four streets over, on Pell Avenue. I drove the ladder there with the back window down and one hand reaching behind to hold it steady, the way my father would have done, because neither of us ever owned a truck.

The man who answered the door was younger than I expected—sixty, maybe, with a neat white beard. He looked at me and then at the ladder leaning against my car and I watched him understand it before I said anything.

"You're Frank's boy."

"I'm returning your ladder."

He nodded slowly. He didn't say *I'm sorry* right away, which I appreciated. He said, "He kept meaning to bring that back. I told him no rush. I don't go up on the roof anymore anyway."

"Then why'd you lend it to him?"

Dave Hollis smiled in a way that went sideways. "Because he asked. Your dad didn't ask for much. He was cleaning your mother's gutters. Not his, hers. The old house on Cardiff."

I hadn't known that. My parents had been divorced for nineteen years. My mother still lived on Cardiff Street and had, as far as I knew, a service that came out every fall.

"He didn't want her to know," Dave said. "He'd go over when she was at her sister's. I guess the service was expensive and she'd complained about it once, at your cousin's wedding, and he just—" He shrugged. "He remembered it."

I put the ladder in his garage. He offered coffee. I said I had things to do, and he nodded like he understood that too.

I didn't call Ruth. I want to be honest about that. I found a Ruth in his phone—there was only one—and I sat with the phone in my hand for a long time and I didn't call, because Thursday had already come and gone several times over and whatever it had been about, I wasn't the one who could do it. I've thought since that this was cowardice, and I've thought since that it was respect, and I've concluded that those two things are closer together than people admit.

I bought the oil. It seemed pointless—the car was going to be sold—but I put it in anyway, in the driveway, on my back on the cold concrete, and I understood while I was under there why he had put it on the list. It's a thing you can do. It has a beginning and an end. The car would run better for someone I'd never meet.

The bank I could not do for him, and the tree I never identified. There is a maple in the front yard that leans slightly toward the house, and I've decided that's the one, and that he meant to ask someone whether it was dangerous. I've decided this because I need the list to have an edge, a place where it stops.

Here is what I keep coming back to. My father was not a sentimental man. He did not write letters or keep photographs in any order. But he wrote *Call Ruth re: Thursday* and *Return ladder to Dave* on the back of an envelope, and in doing so he left a more accurate portrait of himself than anything he could have composed on purpose: a man with a small number of obligations he took seriously, a man who borrowed things and meant to return them, a man who climbed a ladder in secret to clean the gutters of a woman who had not been his wife for nineteen years.

The envelope is in my desk now. I haven't crossed anything off. I've thought about it—the latch, the ladder, the oil—but the pen would be mine and the list is not, and there is a difference, and I think he would have known what it was.
